'''Asama Shrine''' (Sengen Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in Shibamoto-chō, {{ill|Mishima, Shizuoka|Q653478|qid=Q653478}}, {{ill|Shizuoka Prefecture|Q131320|qid=Q131320}}. It was formerly the Sannomiya, later the Ninomiya, of {{ill|Izu Province|Q860928|qid=Q860928}}. It is one of the {{ill|Sengen shrine|Q3471785|qid=Q3471785}} shrines.

=== Overview ===
In ancient times it was one of the eight auxiliary shrines (Hassho Bekū) of {{ill|Mishima Taisha|Q650772|qid=Q650772}}{{Sfn|History of Mishima City, Vol. 2|1988|p=558}}. It was also regarded as a {{ill|Sessha|Q135009904|qid=Q135009904}} (subsidiary shrine), but is now independent.

Although it is listed as a candidate shrine for the Shikinaisha “Iga Muhime no Mikoto Shrine,” it is not considered a leading theory. Generally, this Himusubi no Mikoto Shrine is thought to be the Raiden Shrine, a subsidiary shrine of {{ill|Izusan Shrine|Q611460|qid=Q611460}} in {{ill|Atami|Q653364|qid=Q653364}}, and there is a theory that this shrine served as its distant worship site{{Sfn|Medieval Provincial Ichinomiya System|2000|p=162}}. The shrine name is said to have shifted from the Buddhist name “Sengen” of the honji-butsu (original Buddhist manifestation) of Izusan Shrine—{{ill|Thousand-armed Kannon|Q10904910|qid=Q10904910|lt=Eleven-Faced Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Kannon}}—to the kami name “Asama”{{Sfn|Revised Tōshū Shikō, Vol. 8 (Upper)|p=35}}.

According to the “{{ill|Izumi Province Shrine Rank Register|Q17193087|qid=Q17193087}},” its divine rank is “Senior First Rank, Thousand-Eyed Great Bodhisattva.” It was originally the Sannomiya of Izumi Province, but after the Ninomiya Hachimangū (present-day Wakamiya Shrine) was transferred to the grounds of the grand shrine, it became the Ninomiya{{Sfn|Medieval Provincial Ichinomiya System|2000|p=162}}. However, there is no record that the Shinnomiya, Hirose Shrine, was elevated to Sannomiya{{Sfn|Medieval Provincial Ichinomiya System|2000|p=162}}, and one theory holds that the Sannomiya was Yōhara Shrine{{Sfn|History of Mishima City, Vol. 2|1988|p=559}}.

The annual festival is held on July 15 and 16. It is said that in the past, people always visited this shrine when making a {{ill|mountaineering in Mount Fuji|Q11456115|qid=Q11456115}}. In addition, the spring water around the precincts served as irrigation water for downstream towns and villages.<ref name="various" />

=== Enshrined deities ===
[[File:Sengen-jinja (Mishima, Shizuoka).JPG|thumb|Asama Shrine worship hall]]
* Principal deities
** {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|Q1781862|qid=Q1781862|lt=Konohanasakuya-hime no Mikoto}}
** Hafuhime no Mikoto
* Associated deities
** {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|Q1056017|qid=Q1056017|lt=Ninigi no Mikoto}}
** {{ill|Amenohoakari|Q10940411|qid=Q10940411|lt=Hoakari no Mikoto}}
** {{ill|Hosuseri|Q10731395|qid=Q10731395|lt=Hoderi no Mikoto}}
** {{ill|Hoori|Q1051960|qid=Q1051960|lt=Hoori no Mikoto}}

Konohanasakuya-hime no Mikoto is the daughter of the Mishima Ōkami ({{ill|Ōyamatsumi|lt=Ōyamatsumi|Q386563|qid=Q386563|qid=Q386563|lt=Ōyamatsumi no Mikoto}}), the enshrined deity of Mishima Taisha. According to the “{{ill|Miyake-ki|Q17215100|qid=Q17215100}},” Hafuhime no Mikoto was a consort whom the Mishima Ōkami placed on {{ill|Izu Ōshima|Q1070580|qid=Q1070580|lt=Ōshima}}. Furthermore, the associated deity Ninigi no Mikoto is the husband of Konohanasakuya-hime no Mikoto, and Hoakari no Mikoto, Hoderi no Mikoto, and Hoori no Mikoto are their sons. In other words, the shrine enshrines the wife and daughter of the deity of Mishima Taisha, as well as the daughter’s family.

=== Shrine within the precincts ===
[[File:Shibaoka Shrine.jpg|thumb|Shibaoka Shrine]]
; Shibaoka Shrine
:* Enshrined deity: {{ill|Takamimusubi|UNKNOWN|qid=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi no Kami}}
:* Shrine rank: {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=Village shrine}}
:* Annual festival: July 15–16
: It is enshrined to the left of the main hall of Asama Shrine. Originally, it was a residence shrine enshrined on the estate of the Seko Rokudayū family of the Seko honjin, but in {{ill|Meiji – year 4|Q11512280|qid=Q11512280}} ({{ill|1871|Q7746|qid=Q7746}} or {{ill|1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753}}) it came to be worshiped as the tutelary shrine of Shiba Town and was ranked as a village shrine. In March {{ill|1877|Q7773|qid=Q7773}} (Meiji 10), it was destroyed in the great fire of {{ill|Mishima-shuku|Q524171|qid=Q524171}}, but was restored in {{ill|1880|Q7806|qid=Q7806}} (Meiji 13). In July 1952 it was merged into Asama Shrine and relocated to the present site together with its shrine building. Beneath the main hall is a large circular stone called the “spirit stone,” which is regarded as a guardian deity for children.<ref name="various" />
